titre: Pruitt-Igoe never won the architecture award it is credited with
accroche: Charles Jencks dated the death of modern architecture to the minute, for a building that never received the architecture award he invents for it.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1977, in The Language of Post-Modern Architecture, critic Charles Jencks writes that modern architecture died in St. Louis, Missouri, on July 15, 1972 at 3:32 p.m., when the Pruitt-Igoe public housing complex was given the coup de grâce by dynamite. The line, immediately taken up by generations of historians and critics, fixes in memory a precise moment when modern architecture, embodied by this project, supposedly officially failed.

## An award that never existed

Architectural historian Katharine Bristol has since established that this version barely holds together. Jencks himself presents Pruitt-Igoe as designed according to the most progressive ideas of CIAM, adding that it had received an award from the American Institute of Architects when it was designed in 1951. Bristol checked: Pruitt-Igoe never won any architecture award. The award does exist, but it was given to a different project, the John Cochran Garden Apartments, designed by the same firm in the same St. Louis neighborhood; it simply ended up, over successive retellings, attributed to the wrong building.

The time, for its part, never claimed to be exact. Jencks places the moment at 3:32 p.m., but himself qualifies it with an “or so” in the original text: a veneer of precision, not a measurement.

The invented award is only the symptom of a larger problem. Pruitt-Igoe, 2,700 housing units designed in 1950 by the firm of Minoru Yamasaki, future architect of the World Trade Center towers, saw its innovations, glass-enclosed galleries meant as vertical streets, drained of their substance by budget cuts imposed before construction was even finished. The federal law of 1949 also required public housing authorities to fund the upkeep of their housing solely from the rents collected: when occupancy fell after peaking at 91% in 1957, revenue collapsed with it, and routine maintenance could never again keep up. Completed in 1954, the same year as a Supreme Court ruling ordering desegregation, the project, initially divided into a white half and a Black half, never managed to integrate and became, almost from opening day, an all-Black project.

## What this shifts

By blaming architectural form alone for Pruitt-Igoe's failure, to the point of inventing an award it never received, Jencks's line obscured what political scientist Eugene Meehan called the “programmed failure” of American public housing: structurally insufficient funding, racial segregation that the law itself organized, and a political disinvestment of which the towers were merely the backdrop. Making beams and facades answer for decisions made elsewhere, by others, years earlier, amounts to excusing everyone except architecture from accountability.

carte.punch: Pruitt-Igoe, the symbol of modern architecture's failure, never won a single award.
carte.idee: Charles Jencks dated the death of modern architecture to the demolition of Pruitt-Igoe in 1972, a complex he said had been honored by the AIA. Katharine Bristol showed that it received no award: that honor belonged to another project, the John Cochran Garden Apartments.

quiz.question: What did historian Katharine Bristol discover about the architecture award that Charles Jencks attributes to Pruitt-Igoe in his 1977 text?
choix: The award had indeed been given to Pruitt-Igoe, but was quietly withdrawn after demolition began
Pruitt-Igoe never received this award, which had actually been given to another project by the same firm
The award existed, but had been given to the firm as a whole rather than to this specific project
The award Jencks describes never existed, in any form, at the American Institute of Architects
quiz.explication: Bristol established that Pruitt-Igoe never won an architecture award. The award Jencks invokes had actually been given to the John Cochran Garden Apartments, a neighboring project designed by the same firm, Leinweber, Yamasaki & Hellmuth, and ended up attributed to the wrong building over successive retellings.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the federal law of 1949 provide for funding the upkeep of public housing like Pruitt-Igoe?
choix: Public housing authorities had to fund upkeep solely from the rents collected
The federal government covered all routine maintenance costs
Municipalities had to supplement rents with a dedicated property tax
Neighboring private owners funded part of the upkeep by agreement
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The federal law of 1949 required public housing authorities to fund the upkeep of their housing solely from the rents collected; when occupancy fell after 1957, revenue collapsed with it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which architect, associated with the design of Pruitt-Igoe in 1950, later designed the World Trade Center towers?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Pruitt-Igoe was designed in 1950 by the firm of Minoru Yamasaki, who would later become the architect of the World Trade Center towers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the expression “programmed failure,” used about Pruitt-Igoe, refer to, according to this card?
choix: A design flaw that Yamasaki himself supposedly acknowledged before the demolition
A term invented by Charles Jencks to describe the 1972 demolition
A set of political and financial causes that predate architectural form alone
A contractual clause limiting the building's planned lifespan to twenty years
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The expression, used by political scientist Eugene Meehan, refers to insufficient funding, segregation organized by law, and political disinvestment, not a flaw in architectural form alone.
